title: Getting started
goal: Run your first Python file and create an isolated working environment.
body:
You need Python 3.12 or 3.13, VS Code or PyCharm, and a terminal. Basic HTML knowledge is useful. This course uses Django 5.2 and SQLite. The small practice CMS is a separate learning project; you will explore AgentCMS in the final module. No AI API key is needed.

1. Create a project folder

Windows · Command Prompt (cmd)
Terminal
mkdir designit-python
cd designit-python
py -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
python --version
macOS / Linux
Terminal
mkdir designit-python
cd designit-python
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python --version

Select .venv as the Python interpreter in your editor. The rest of the course uses python in the activated environment. On Windows, use Command Prompt if PowerShell blocks the activation script.

Create hello.py
name = "DesignIT"
print(f"Hello from {name}!")
Terminal
python hello.py

Expected output: Hello from DesignIT!. Python runs on your computer. This web course displays code but does not execute Python in the browser.
task: Change the message and run the file again. Find out which Python interpreter your editor is using.
answer: A virtual environment keeps the project’s packages separate from those of other projects. It is not a database or a web server.

title: Variables and data types
goal: Represent CMS content using text, numbers, and Boolean values.
body:
A variable gives a value a name. Python uses str for text, int for whole numbers, and bool for true/false values. Unlike JavaScript, Python writes True and False with capital initial letters. Indentation is part of the syntax.

Create basics.py
title = "About us"
views_count = 12
published = False
views_count += 1
print(f"{title}: {views_count} views")
print(type(published).__name__)

Run python basics.py. You should see About us: 13 views and bool. The = sign assigns a value; == compares two values.
task: Add a variable called author. Use an f-string to display the author, title, and publication status.
check: Is the string "False" the same as the value False?
answer: No. "False" is text, while False is a Boolean value. A non-empty string is also treated as true in an if condition.

title: Conditions and loops
goal: Filter a collection so that only published content is displayed.
body:
An if statement expresses a rule. A for loop processes one item at a time. Use four spaces for each indentation level. A list collects items; a dictionary associates field names with values.

Create publishing.py
pages = [
    {"title": "Home", "published": True},
    {"title": "New idea", "published": False},
]
for page in pages:
    if page["published"]:
        print(page["title"])
    else:
        print("Hidden draft")

The output is Home and Hidden draft. Later, the same publication rule must be enforced on the server. Hiding a link in HTML is not enough to protect a draft.
task: Add a published page called Contact. Then change the loop so that drafts produce no output.
check: Which lines must be inside the if block?
answer: All actions that should happen only when the page is published. Python determines this from indentation, not curly brackets.

title: Functions and debugging
goal: Write reusable logic and understand a simple error message.
body:
A function accepts parameters and can return a value. print displays something in the terminal; return sends a result back to the code that called the function.

Create functions.py
def display_title(title):
    clean = title.strip()
    if not clean:
        raise ValueError("Title must not be empty")
    return clean.upper()

print(display_title("  About us  "))
try:
    print(display_title("   "))
except ValueError as error:
    print(f"Invalid content: {error}")

You should see ABOUT US followed by an explanatory message. Read a traceback from the bottom: the error type and message, then the file and line number. Handle expected errors explicitly; do not hide every error with an empty except block.
task: Change the function so that it preserves the title’s letter case. Explain what strip() does before running the code.
check: What does a function without return return?
answer: It returns None. Output from print is not the function’s return value.

title: Data, JSON, and classes
goal: Distinguish data exchange from a model that also defines behaviour.
body:
A dictionary describes a record in memory. JSON is a text format for storing and exchanging data. A class combines structure and behaviour; Django models build on this idea. You do not need to master all of object-oriented programming before continuing.

Create data.py
import json
from pathlib import Path

page = {"title": "Home", "published": True}
file = Path("page.json")
file.write_text(json.dumps(page, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
loaded = json.loads(file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
print(loaded["title"])

class Page:
    def __init__(self, title):
        self.title = title

    def label(self):
        return f"Page: {self.title}"

print(Page(loaded["title"]).label())

JSON uses true; Python uses True. The json module translates between them. self refers to the current object. Imports bring in tools from other modules. The file page.json is not a database.
task: Save two pages as a list in JSON and read them back. Print their titles using a loop.
check: Why use json.loads rather than eval to read JSON?
answer: json.loads interprets JSON as data. eval can execute Python code and should not be used to read JSON.

title: Django: from URL to response
goal: Start a project and understand URLs, views, and HTTP responses.
body:
A Django project contains settings and one or more apps. An app groups a subject area, such as CMS pages. The browser sends an HTTP request; the URL configuration selects a view that returns a response. Python runs on the server, while the browser receives HTML.

Terminal · in designit-python, with .venv activated
python -m pip install "Django>=5.2,<5.3"
python -m django startproject config .
python manage.py startapp pages
python manage.py migrate

Open config/settings.py. Add "pages", to the existing INSTALLED_APPS list. Keep the default apps. Leave the SQLite configuration unchanged.

pages/views.py · replace the contents
from django.http import HttpResponse

def index(request):
    return HttpResponse("Hello from your first CMS!")
config/urls.py · replace the contents
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path
from pages import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("admin/", admin.site.urls),
    path("", views.index, name="index"),
]
Terminal
python manage.py runserver

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/. You should see the greeting. Stop the server with Ctrl+C before entering more commands in the same terminal. runserver is for local development only; Google Sites cannot run Django.
task: Change the greeting. Locate the function that receives request and the line that connects it to the home page.
check: What is the difference between the config project and the pages app?
answer: config contains the project’s shared settings and URLs. pages groups the CMS functionality. One project can contain several apps.

title: Models, databases, and admin
goal: Create a Page model and edit content in Django admin.
body:
A model describes data to be stored. The Django ORM lets you work with the database using Python. A migration describes a change to the database structure. Admin provides an editing interface for registered models.

pages/models.py · replace the contents
from django.db import models

class Page(models.Model):
    title = models.CharField(max_length=200)
    slug = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    body = models.TextField(blank=True)
    published = models.BooleanField(default=False)

    def __str__(self):
        return self.title
pages/admin.py · replace the contents
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Page

@admin.register(Page)
class PageAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ("title", "slug", "published")
    list_filter = ("published",)
    prepopulated_fields = {"slug": ("title",)}
Terminal
python manage.py makemigrations pages
python manage.py migrate
python manage.py createsuperuser
python manage.py runserver

Choose your own username and password in the terminal. Sign in at http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/. Create Home with the slug home and published checked, and New idea with the slug new-idea and published unchecked. Use practice content only. A slug is a URL-friendly identifier.
task: Create both pages in admin. Change body and check that the content is still present after restarting.
check: How does makemigrations differ from migrate?
answer: makemigrations creates migration files from model changes. migrate applies those migrations to the database.

title: Display content with templates
goal: Connect a model, view, and HTML to create a small working CMS.
body:
A view retrieves data, and a template determines its HTML presentation. We filter published pages in both the list and the detail view. This also prevents a visitor from opening a draft by guessing its URL.

pages/views.py · replace the contents
from django.shortcuts import get_object_or_404, render
from .models import Page

def index(request):
    pages = Page.objects.filter(published=True).order_by("title")
    return render(request, "pages/index.html", {"pages": pages})

def detail(request, slug):
    page = get_object_or_404(Page, slug=slug, published=True)
    return render(request, "pages/detail.html", {"page": page})
config/urls.py · replace the contents
from django.contrib import admin
from django.urls import path
from pages import views

urlpatterns = [
    path("admin/", admin.site.urls),
    path("", views.index, name="index"),
    path("pages/<slug:slug>/", views.detail, name="detail"),
]

Create the folders pages/templates/pages/ in your editor. Create the two files below. The default APP_DIRS=True setting allows Django to find them when pages is registered in INSTALLED_APPS.

pages/templates/pages/index.html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>My CMS</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Published pages</h1>
  <ul>
    {% for page in pages %}
      <li><a href="{% url 'detail' page.slug %}">{{ page.title }}</a></li>
    {% empty %}
      <li>No published pages yet.</li>
    {% endfor %}
  </ul>
</body>
</html>
pages/templates/pages/detail.html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>{{ page.title }}</title></head>
<body>
  <a href="{% url 'index' %}">All pages</a>
  <h1>{{ page.title }}</h1>
  {{ page.body|linebreaks }}
</body>
</html>

Start the server again. The home page should list Home. /pages/home/ displays its text, while /pages/new-idea/ returns 404. Templates escape text automatically; do not apply the safe filter to untrusted content.
task: Publish and unpublish New idea in admin. Test both the home page and the direct URL after each change.
check: Where should the publication rule be enforced?
answer: On the server when retrieving data. Hiding the draft’s link in the template does not prevent direct access.

title: Test the rules before moving on
goal: Document expected behaviour with automated Django tests.
body:
A test translates an expectation into a check that can be repeated. TestClient sends requests without runserver running. Django TestCase uses a separate test database. The tests below cover publication, drafts, and missing pages.

pages/tests.py · replace the contents
from django.test import TestCase
from django.urls import reverse
from .models import Page

class PublicationTests(TestCase):
    @classmethod
    def setUpTestData(cls):
        Page.objects.create(title="Home", slug="home", published=True)
        Page.objects.create(title="Secret draft", slug="draft")

    def test_only_published_in_index(self):
        response = self.client.get(reverse("index"))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)
        self.assertContains(response, "Home")
        self.assertNotContains(response, "Secret draft")

    def test_published_detail(self):
        response = self.client.get(reverse("detail", args=["home"]))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 200)

    def test_draft_detail_is_404(self):
        response = self.client.get(reverse("detail", args=["draft"]))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)

    def test_missing_detail_is_404(self):
        response = self.client.get(reverse("detail", args=["does-not-exist"]))
        self.assertEqual(response.status_code, 404)
Terminal
python manage.py check
python manage.py test

All four tests should pass. Experiment: remove published=True from the detail lookup, run the tests, and observe the failing draft test. Restore the filter before continuing. Passing tests do not replace code review or manual exploration.
task: Explain in your own words which user rule each test protects. Run the experiment and restore the working code.
check: Why test a direct URL to a draft?
answer: A list can look correct even when its detail view exposes unpublished content. These are two different entry points.

title: From CMS to Spec-Driven Development
goal: Write a verifiable specification and use a coding agent for a focused change.
body:
In specification-driven development, you describe the desired behaviour, boundaries, and acceptance criteria before implementation. A coding agent can help with analysis, planning, code, and tests. You remain responsible for checking whether the result meets the need. This workflow is independent of any particular tool and can be used with Copilot, Codex, or Claude Code.

First: get to know AgentCMS

Open the AgentCMS page and the repository it links to: vicnorm/AgentCMS. The page describes a Django CMS with a page builder and hardcoded settings for the name, fonts, and colour, among other things. We have not verified the repository’s current file structure. Do not assume that the practice project’s Page model or file names exist there.

  1. Create your own fork or local copy. Read the current README, Python version, and dependencies. Follow the repository’s installation instructions in a separate virtual environment.
  2. Run the system and its existing tests before making changes. Locate settings, models, admin, views, templates, and any page builder. Record actual file paths and the current commit.
  3. Choose one need: an editable site name in admin. If it already exists, choose another small improvement and update the specification.
First prompt · analysis only
Inspect this repository without changing code. Read the README and dependencies.
Find where the site name is defined and used in the header and HTML title.
Report actual file paths and relevant symbols. Locate existing tests
and provide the commands to run them. Separate observations from assumptions.
Suggest one small change and list questions that need to be resolved.

Write spec.md before asking for code

Example · adapt after analysing the repository
# Editable site name
## Need
As an editor, I want to change the site name in Django admin without editing code.
## Scope
Only the site name in the header and HTML title. No colour picker,
font changes, page-builder changes, API, or AI integration.
## Acceptance criteria
AC1: Staff with the required model permission can save a name of 1–80
characters after trimming; admin rejects an empty name or 81 characters.
AC2: Anonymous users and signed-in users without the required permission
cannot change the name through admin.
AC3: The saved name appears in the header and HTML title of affected public
pages on a new request and remains available after a restart.
AC4: If no configuration has been saved, the current default name is used.
AC5: The name is rendered as escaped text, including when it contains HTML characters.
## Technical constraints
Reuse the repository’s configuration pattern if one exists.
Register any new model in admin and provide the required migration.
No new dependencies. No changes to existing publication rules.
## Verification
Map at least one concrete check to each AC. Run existing and new tests.
Document a manual check of the name and persistence after a restart.
## Open questions before implementation
Which templates are affected? Does a configuration model already exist?
Should the name be shared across all pages? Resolve these before coding.

Plan → small changes → verification

Second prompt · after resolving the questions
Read spec.md and the repository analysis. Create plan.md with affected files,
migrations, permissions, and a test for each AC. Do not implement yet.
Once I have reviewed the plan, implement one step at a time.
Preserve the repository’s versions and patterns. Report changed files,
commands actually run, and their results; do not claim tests were run
if they were not. Explain deviations before expanding the scope.

Review the plan, ask the agent to implement it, read the diff, and run the checks yourself. Finally, create review.md with AC1–AC5, test results, manual observations, and any deviations. Spec.md, plan.md, and review.md form a simple course workflow; they do not require a particular SDD product.

Deliverables

  • Repository analysis with file paths and a recorded starting point.
  • A specification, plan, and small code change with any required migration.
  • Test results and a manual demonstration against the criteria.
  • A short reflection: What did AI suggest, what did you change, and why?

If you cannot run AgentCMS, implement the same specification in the practice CMS. Label the submission as a practice implementation. It is not a verified change to AgentCMS.
task: Write your own specification with one need and 3–5 testable criteria. Map each criterion to a test or a documented manual check.
check: What makes a specification more useful than “make a nicer CMS page”?
answer: It makes the need, scope, and expected behaviour concrete and verifiable. You can assess whether the solution is correct before judging how impressive it looks.
